entry.rationale: Thomas Flynn (head of household in 1850 and 1860 censuses) should appear in 1870 with all household members named. At this date Patrick (~25) may still be in or near the household, but more critically Thomas Flynn's wife — Patrick's candidate mother — would appear by name for the first time in any record we have searched. The household also identifies siblings still at home, creating a FAN cluster whose own records (items 3, 4, 6, and 7) can independently corroborate parentage. FamilySearch indexes the 1870 census free of charge. Variant spellings Flynn/Flinn/Flyn should be searched.

The 1880 census is the first federal enumeration to record each person's explicit relationship to the head of household. Thomas Flynn (b. ~1815–1825) would be ~55–65 in 1880 and likely still alive; his wife's relationship ('wife') and any children still at home ('son'/'daughter') would be stated outright rather than inferred from co-residence. This is the strongest household-structure record available before civil registration began in 1906 (loc_001). The 1880 census is fully indexed and free on FamilySearch. If Thomas is absent (deceased by 1880), his widow's household and surname are still valuable FAN evidence.

Patrick's siblings — identified from the 1870/1880 census household (items 1–2) — who survived past 1906 will have Pennsylvania state death certificates naming their parents directly. Pennsylvania began statewide civil death registration in 1906 (loc_001); these certificates carry a field for the deceased's father and mother. A sibling's death certificate naming Thomas Flynn and his wife provides independent, direct evidence of the same parentage, correcting for the weakness of Patrick's own 1908 death certificate (secondary-quality: informant was son-in-law James Brown, who also mis-stated Patrick's birthplace). Date window set to siblings' plausible lifespans: born ~1840–1865, dying 1906–1950.

Patrick was born ~1845 in Ireland (per 1860 census; the death certificate's 'Pennsylvania' is secondary quality from an uninformed informant), so his own baptism is an Irish record. However, younger siblings born after the family arrived in Schuylkill County (~1846 onward) would have been baptized locally. Catholic parish baptismal registers name both parents at the moment of baptism — primary information from a person of firsthand knowledge (the priest). The SYNTH-PA-CHURCH collection (1708–1985, ~982K persons) is indexed on FamilySearch. Search for Flynn/Flinn baptisms 1847–1865 with Thomas Flynn as father. Per loc_001, parishes fell under the Diocese of Philadelphia until 1868, then the Diocese of Scranton; both should be checked.

Browse-only image group 007936751 (187 images, 0% record-searchable) covers Schuylkill County church records 1842–1895 — the full period when Thomas Flynn's family would have been baptizing children and when Thomas and his wife may have married locally. As loc_001 notes, some church and naturalization films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups not reachable by a record_search. This item requires image-by-image browsing for Flynn/Flinn entries. Fallback for item 4 (indexed church search): if the SYNTH-PA-CHURCH indexed search yields nothing for Flynn baptisms or the Thomas Flynn marriage, browse this unindexed volume before concluding the church record avenue is exhausted.

FAN item — targets Patrick's siblings, not Patrick himself. Browse-only image group 007936753 (94 images, 0% record-searchable) covers Schuylkill County marriage records 1870–1910. Pennsylvania marriage applications required the parties to state their parents' names; a sibling's marriage record names Thomas Flynn and his wife as the sibling's parents, providing the same parentage evidence independently of Patrick's own records. The siblings and their approximate marriage dates will be derived from the 1870/1880 census results (items 1–2). Requires image-by-image browsing; Flynn/Flinn name variants should be checked.

FAN item — targets Thomas Flynn's community witnesses and his own stated origin. Browse-only image group 007936750 (298 images, 0% record-searchable) covers Schuylkill County naturalization records 1849–1915. Irish immigrants who naturalized through the Court of Common Pleas filed a Declaration of Intent ('first papers') and a Petition for Naturalization ('second papers'). The petition names the petitioner's age, country and often county/townland of birth, U.S. arrival date, and two witnesses. Witnesses are typically relatives or close neighbors — the FAN cluster surrounding Thomas Flynn. Finding his naturalization papers could (a) name his origin in Ireland, enabling a future search of Irish records; and (b) identify witnesses who are FAN members with their own records. Date window ends at 1870 since Thomas should be naturalized by then to head a household; records up to 1870 are most relevant.

The indexed FamilySearch probate search for Thomas Flynn (pli_006, pl_002) returned no results for 1870–1900. Browse-only image group 007936749 (412 images, 0% record-searchable) covers Schuylkill County probate 1851–1930 — a wider time window and a different access method. Thomas may have died intestate (producing an administration rather than a will), or the index may have missed him under a spelling variant (Flinn, Flyn, Flynt). Browse-image access may surface his estate file or an intestate administration naming his heirs — direct evidence of Patrick's parentage. Date window extended to 1930 to allow for Thomas dying later in life. Thomas's lifespan bounds this window: as household head in 1850, he was probably born ~1815–1825 and could plausibly have lived to ~1900–1910.

Image group 007936752 (543 images, 22% record-searchable) covers Schuylkill County deed records 1815–1900. Land transfers name the grantor and grantee; if Thomas Flynn conveyed property during his lifetime, his name appears and can confirm identity and residence. If he died holding property, his heirs (named in the deed from the estate) provide direct evidence of the family structure — including Patrick's status as a son. Deeds also establish the last date Thomas Flynn transacted, narrowing the window for his death and focusing the probate search (item 8). At 22% indexed, a partial record search is possible; remaining images require browsing. Date window is set by Thomas Flynn's plausible lifespan as household head in 1850 (born ~1815–1825, likely died by ~1905–1910).

entry.rationale: A pre-existing (uncited) FamilySearch tree source claims 'M M Wood' was the household head in the 1860 Blount County, AL census. Martha was born ~1859 in Georgia; if she appears as an infant in that household, the head of household is her father and the wife is her mother. FamilySearch volume 005154190 is 99% name-indexed and full-text searchable, making this a low-cost, high-yield search. Corroborating this unverified tree lead is the essential first step before any parentage conclusion can rest on the 'Wood' surname. Variant spellings: Woods, Woode. All household members, ages, birthplaces, and neighboring households should be recorded as FAN leads.

The 1869 Smith County marriage record records the bride as 'M J Wood', but 'Wood' is her birth surname only if the Lanham marriage was her first. A prior marriage under a different surname would invalidate the Wood parentage hypothesis entirely. Smith County marriage volumes 1857-1876 (FamilySearch volume 007255720) are 100% name-indexed and full-text searchable — searching for any Wood bride before 7 Jan 1869 is straightforward. Additionally, the full original image of the 7 Jan 1869 record should be obtained to identify the bondsman or witness, who was frequently the bride's father or brother (a direct FAN lead to Martha's parents under Standard 14).

Per the record-type guide, a parentage plan must include a dedicated search for the parents' own marriage record. A marriage record confirms the couple as a unit, supplies the mother's maiden name (which census records omit), and by its date relative to Martha's birth (~1859) corroborates the father otherwise named only by census co-residence. Additionally, marriages of Wood siblings in Blount County would name the same parents and serve as corroborating parentage evidence. FamilySearch volume 007316662 covers Blount County marriages 1820-1888 and is 80-100% name-indexed and full-text searchable.

The 1870 federal census is the first census after Martha's January 1869 marriage to W F Lanham. It should confirm her age (consistent with ~1859 birth) and birthplace (Georgia), strengthening her identity link to the Alabama/Georgia Wood family. Per Standard 14, neighboring households should also be recorded: Wood family members appearing in the same neighborhood are a direct FAN lead that may identify her parents or siblings who migrated to Texas alongside her family.

Martha was born in Georgia ~1859, but the family appears in Alabama in the 1860 census. The 1850 census would show the family in an earlier location — possibly still in Georgia — establishing the migration timeline. A Wood household in 1850 Georgia or Alabama would supply the father's full name, approximate birth year, and older siblings' names. The 1840 census (if the father was born ~1815-1825) would show the grandfather generation. FamilySearch collection 2016756 (Alabama Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810-1890) covers both decades for Alabama. Per Standard 12, historical migration patterns must inform plan scope.

If the 1850 Alabama census (item 5) does not find the Wood family in Blount County, or if the 1860 census household was recently arrived from Georgia, a direct search of the 1850 U.S. Census for Georgia is needed. Martha was born in Georgia ~1859, so the family resided in Georgia through at least 1858-1859. A Wood household in 1850 Georgia with children consistent with the 1860 Alabama picture would establish the Georgia county of origin, which is required to search Georgia church, marriage, and probate records. Per Standard 17, reasonably exhaustive research requires tracing the family to their Georgia origins.

Alabama had no civil vital records before 1908; probate records are the primary substitute for identifying family relationships. A father's will naming his children as heirs is direct parentage evidence. FamilySearch volume 004808801 covers Blount County probate records 1845-1957 and is full-text searchable (though only ~2% name-indexed), so keyword search on 'Wood' combined with 'Martha', 'Mattie', or 'M J' is the required strategy. This item also covers guardianship files, which would name a minor child's parents if the father died while Martha was young. Use the search-full-text skill for co-occurrence keyword search.

Per Standard 14, a parentage plan must cast a wide FAN net. If Martha's father or a Wood family member migrated to Hill County, Texas (where Martha settled after the 1879 Neal marriage), an estate file might name her as heir or next of kin. FamilySearch volume 004820309 (Hill County probate case files 1853-1935) is full-text searchable but only ~3% name-indexed — keyword search on 'Wood' and 'Lanham' is required. This is the Texas counterpart to the Alabama probate item and covers the possibility that the Wood family followed Martha to Texas.

Cemetery records are a key substitute for civil vital records in pre-1908 Alabama. A Wood family burial cluster in Blount County would provide birth and death dates, and family headstone groupings often link parents to children. If a Wood father and mother are buried together with a gravestone naming their children or noting that their daughter Martha married into the Lanham/Neal families, that is corroborating parentage evidence. This is an external repository (FindAGrave.com) identified in the locality survey. Per Standard 13, plans must follow leads to original records wherever possible; cemetery records are original-source evidence for dates and often for family relationships.

dimensions.name: Correctness
dimensions.rationale: The plan's factual claims are accurate and well-supported. The plan correctly identifies Martha's documented surnames (Wood, Landham, Neal, Hamby), accurately cites the 1869 Smith County marriage record and the uncited tree source, correctly notes the absence of Alabama civil vital records before 1908 and Texas before 1903, and accurately describes the indexing status and searchability of FamilySearch volumes (e.g., 1860 Blount County census 99% indexed, Smith County marriage 100% indexed, Blount County probate ~2% indexed). All nine items target real record types and jurisdictions that existed in the specified periods. The plan correctly incorporates locality survey information (Blount County quirks, Texas marriage volumes, FindAGrave as external resource). No fabricated material or unsupported claims are present.

dimensions.name: Completeness
dimensions.rationale: The plan addresses all required elements for a first research plan on q_002. It creates a new active plan (pl_001) with nine sequenced items, establishes fallback chains (pli_006 fallback_for pli_005), includes both direct-naming items (marriage records, probate, cemetery) and verification items (Smith County marriage search to test whether Wood is birth surname), spans appropriate jurisdictions (Alabama, Texas, Georgia), and covers multiple record types (census, marriage, probate, cemetery). The plan includes rationales explaining why each item advances the parentage question. No major omissions of required work are present.

## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been located. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.
Roman Catholic parishes fell under the Diocese of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Scranton was erected in 1868; sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

items.rationale: 1850 census fully indexed on FamilySearch. Free access, start here.
Ancestry has independent indexing; cross-check for transcription errors.
Third independent index for coverage confirmation.
